paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disorder that begins in the first weeks of life. Affected infants cannot absorb dietary glucose and galactose from the intestine, which causes severe diarrhea and dehydration. The disorder is usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991; Martin et al., 1996).

checks.evidence_quote: Glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is an autosomal recessive disease

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption begins in the first weeks of life.
checks.evidence_quote: manifesting within the first weeks of life

checks.claim: Infants with glucose/galactose malabsorption cannot absorb dietary glucose and galactose from the intestine.

checks.claim: Intestinal malabsorption of glucose and galactose in glucose/galactose malabsorption causes severe diarrhea and dehydration.

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is usually fatal unless glucose and galactose are removed from the diet.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) studied glucose transport in jejunal mucosa in vitro in a 3-year-old girl with GGM, her family, and normal volunteers. Mucosa from 6 normal controls and from the proband's asymptomatic 5-year-old brother accumulated glucose to 16 times the concentration in the incubation medium. The proband's mucosa could not concentrate glucose at any point during a 60-minute incubation. Both parents and a half sister had impaired glucose transport, with values between those of normal subjects and the proband. In these heterozygotes, glucose influx was impaired, but glucose efflux from the mucosa was identical to that in 3 normal controls. Kinetic analysis showed a reduced capacity (Vmax) and a normal affinity (Km) for glucose transport. All subjects accumulated fructose similarly. Renal glucose titration showed a partial defect in renal glucose reabsorption in the proband. Her brother's titration curve was similar to those of 7 normal volunteers.

paragraphs.text: Xin and Wang (2011) found a homozygous c.1673G-A transition in the SLC5A1 gene, resulting in an arg558-to-his (R558H) substitution, in Old Order Amish patients with GGM.
